Post-correction, power factor rises to 99.5 percent. The reactive circulating current is eliminated. Voltage stability improves. Motor and compressor equipment operates closer to nameplate conditions. The thermal burden drops. And the cooling system recovers capacity it is currently spending on waste. T10.voltage_stability_findings:

That average alone — sitting roughly 23 volts below nameplate — indicates the field is chronically operating below its design setpoint. But the average understates the risk.

The documented minimum voltage of 9.1 volts confirms at least one full collapse event during the month. That is not a transient sag or a momentary dip. That is a field going to near-zero — a hard outage. The BT chart confirms this with a single gold vertical streak in the 260621–260622 window, estimated at approximately 60 to 90 minutes of total downtime. For a refrigeration and air chiller system, even a one-hour outage carries product safety and process recovery implications that extend well beyond the duration of the event itself.

The four labeled triangular voltage-drop events in the V view are equally important. These dips — measured at 434 to 437 volts — represent sags of 43 to 46 volts below nominal, which is a 9 to nearly 10 percent undervoltage condition. They occur in two distinct clusters: one near the opening of the month around June 1st, and a second cluster in the June 18–19 window. The clustering is not random. It suggests a recurring operational trigger — likely compressor staging, fan load sequencing, or chiller startup events — that is pulling the field down in a patterned way.

For the motors and compressors on this transformer, undervoltage operation in the 434–437 volt range means they are drawing higher current to maintain torque. Higher current means more winding heat. More winding heat means accelerating insulation aging. The voltage minimum tooltip confirms 434 volts as the floor of these labeled events, and the peak current reading of 1,905.4 amps in the V view — against an average of 986.7 amps — shows the compensating current surge that follows each voltage dip. A nearly two-to-one peak-to-average current ratio on a refrigeration transformer is a significant mechanical stress indicator. Without field correction, each recurring dip event is shortening the service life of the equipment connected to this bus.

Two H490 units at 800 kVAR total compensation capacity are the recommended configuration for T10. The installation site at Cherry Avenue should be assessed for switchgear proximity, ventilation adequacy, and physical placement relative to the transformer secondary bus. The 776 kVAR peak demand leaves minimal margin if reactive loads grow — confirm that the H490 pair provides sufficient headroom for seasonal load escalation in Fresno's summer cooling peak.

The two clustering windows of triangular voltage drops — early June and June 18–19 — warrant operational investigation. Identify what load sequences, compressor staging events, or switching operations are occurring in those windows. The voltage is sagging 43 to 46 volts below nominal on a repeating basis, which is causing elevated current draw and motor stress. Short-term mitigation may involve load sequencing adjustment; long-term correction requires MPTS installation to remove the reactive burden that amplifies these sag events.

The 10.4 percent iTHD peak observed in the M view exceeds the IEEE 519 recommended limit of 8 percent. Consider whether passive harmonic filtering should be evaluated alongside MPTS installation, particularly if variable frequency drives are present on this bus.

**4. Outage root cause analysis — Priority: Moderate**
The single confirmed outage event in the June 21–22 window — estimated at 60 to 90 minutes — produced a near-zero voltage reading of 9.1 volts. For a refrigeration and air chiller system, that duration of outage carries product safety implications. Determine whether the outage was utility-side, transformer protection-initiated, or process-related. Implement event logging to capture the triggering condition.

**5. Month-over-month drift monitoring — Priority: Ongoing**
This is an untuned field. Without tuning assignment, the reactive burden, thermal stress, and efficiency losses on T10 are likely to worsen through the summer months. Establish a monthly field health review cadence and flag for escalation if the power factor floor drops below 83 percent, if kVAR MAX exceeds 850 kVAR, or if the thermal burden baseline climbs above 500,000 BTU per hour.

T16.reactive_harmonic_findings:
**T16 Compressor — Reactive and Harmonic Findings | June 2026**

The reactive picture on T16 is large, persistent, and unmanaged. The BT header records an average reactive load of 547.9 kVAR with a dataset maximum of 957.3 kVAR. The M view confirms a labeled peak of 675 kVAR during active production. These are not spikes — the green kVAR layer in both the BT and M views runs as a continuous band through every production period. Reactive energy is structural to how this compressor load operates. It does not go away between cycles. It is present in every production hour, drawing transformer capacity and generating heat without delivering usable work.

The power factor numbers anchor this clearly. At 88.9% average, T16 is operating with roughly 11% of its electromagnetic capacity dedicated to maintaining the reactive field rather than delivering real power. At the minimum recorded power factor of 0.0% — which aligns with the field collapse event — the transformer was momentarily delivering no real power at all while still drawing current. During normal production, the minimum measured PF is 84.7%, recorded during the deepest reactive stress intervals.

The harmonic picture adds another layer. The M view header confirms 3.7% iTHD (current total harmonic distortion) on average, with a maximum of 27.9% iTHD. That maximum is significant. IEEE 519 guidelines set an industrial current distortion limit of 5% at the point of common coupling for many utility interconnection agreements. An iTHD maximum of 27.9% means that at peak harmonic events, this field is producing distortion current at more than five times that threshold. Harmonic currents add to the RMS current burden, increase transformer core losses, generate additional heat in neutral conductors, and can interfere with metering and protective relay accuracy.

The combination of 957.3 kVAR reactive maximum and 27.9% iTHD maximum is particularly stressful for the transformer core and winding insulation. Both reactive current and harmonic current produce heat without contributing to real work output. They are, in effect, two independent mechanisms of thermal waste operating simultaneously on T16.

MPTS sizing for this transformer is driven by the kVAR MAX of 957.3 kVAR. Applying the Unity sizing rule — 957.3 ÷ 400, rounded up — yields a requirement for **3 H490 units**.
